newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's powerful union votes for protest strike.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's powerful union votes for protest strike.

text.p: Members of South Korea's second largest umbrella labour union on Wednesday voted overwhelmingly to strike in protest at plans to revise labour laws that they believe threaten jobs, a union spokesman said.
Chung Sung-hee, a spokesman for the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, said 251,764 members at about 300 companies voted on a proposal to strike this month.
Around 90 percent voted in favour of industrial action, although the exact result would not be known until Thursday, he said. The timing would be decided by union leaders on Friday.
"The first strike is likely to be next week," he said. It would be token action lasting several hours but followed by an all-out strike unless worker demands were met.
Chung said unions that voted to go on strike represented Hyundai Motor Co, South Korea's largest car maker, Kia Motors Corp, Hyundai Heavy Industries Co and Daewoo Heavy Industries Co.
Together, the 300 companies account for the bulk of South Korea's production of vehicles, ships and other key exports. A strike would be a heavy blow to the economy, already hit by an export slump.
On Tuesday the government unveiled plans to revise labour legislation, saying the aim was to end authoritarian controls and help companies improve competitiveness.
The confederation objects to articles that open the way to worker layoffs and flexible working hours.

It claims membership of around 500,000 and is one of two umbrella union organisations along with the Federation of Korea Trade Unions, which represents more than 800 companies and is authorised by the government.
The Korean Confederation would become legal under the proposed revisions. It welcomes moves to end a ban on trade union political activity and allow outside intervention in labour disputes.
But it opposes an article allowing companies to lay off employees to introduce new technology, improve productivity or overcome financial difficulties.
It also objects to a clause permitting companies to introduce flexible work hours to take account of seasonal demand for goods and services.
Officials say the government tried to protect jobs by requiring companies to make every attempt to avoid layoffs and inform workers at least 60 days in advance of any downsizing.

The proposed revision makes clear that workers may not claim wages for the period they are on strike. Many South Korean companies pay wages after strikes are settled in the interests of labour harmony.
Multiple union representation would be sanctioned in each workplace, a key demand of unionised workers. Currently, only one union may represent workers at each company.
Although this reform would not take effect until 2002, leading business groups and the Korea Employers' Federation say they want it withdrawn.

"In view of our country's labour conditions, rival unions would seek to take radical steps to attract more membership if more than a union is allowed in one workplace," an Employers' Federation statement said.
Economists said ending fierce confrontation between union and management is crucial for improving South Korea's industrial competitiveness.
